title: The Case for European Industrials in a Fragmented Supply Chain World
excerpt: As nearshoring accelerates and defence spending rises across NATO members, a cohort of overlooked European capital goods companies are quietly repricing. We examine three names trading below replacement value with defensible moats.
content:
As nearshoring accelerates and defence spending rises across NATO members, a cohort of overlooked European capital goods companies are quietly repricing.

The thesis is straightforward: years of underinvestment in European manufacturing capacity, combined with a structural shift away from single-source supply chains, is creating a demand environment that consensus estimates have consistently underpriced.

We examine three names trading below replacement value with defensible moats and management teams that have demonstrated capital discipline through multiple cycles.

**The macro backdrop**

Defence budgets across NATO are converging toward the 2% GDP target — a level not seen since the Cold War. This is not a temporary spike but a structural rerating of risk that will sustain capex cycles well beyond the typical order book horizon.

Simultaneously, European industrial policy is actively subsidising domestic production of semiconductors, clean energy equipment, and precision components. The IRA's European equivalent is less headline-grabbing but similarly consequential for asset utilisation rates.

**Valuation**

The three companies we are initiating on trade at an average EV/Replacement Cost of 0.87x — a discount to book that historically has resolved upward within 18-24 months in similar macro environments.

We see 35-55% upside to fair value on a 2-year horizon with limited downside given the tangible asset backing.

title: Semiconductor Cycle: Where Are We Really?
excerpt: Inventory corrections are nearly complete in most end-markets. But the AI infrastructure build-out is masking underlying demand weakness in consumer silicon.
content:
Inventory corrections are nearly complete in most end-markets. But the AI infrastructure build-out is masking underlying demand weakness in consumer silicon.

The bifurcation between data centre and consumer end-markets has never been more pronounced. Leading-edge logic capacity is sold out through 2026 for AI accelerator production, while consumer DRAM and NAND pricing continues to find a floor.

**What the data says**

Channel inventory weeks have normalised to 8-10 weeks across most categories — back in line with historical averages after the 2022-2023 correction. But sell-through data tells a more nuanced story: units are moving, but average selling prices in consumer categories remain 15-20% below peak.

This matters for margin recovery timelines. Revenue may trough in H1 2025, but gross margin recovery is a 2026 story for most memory producers.

**Positioning**

We remain selective. Equipment names with AI data centre exposure are fully valued. Memory producers offer asymmetric recovery upside but require patience. Fabless companies with diversified end-market exposure and strong design win pipelines offer the most attractive risk-reward.

title: Why Consensus Price Targets Are Usually Wrong
excerpt: Sell-side price targets are anchored to the current price far more than analysts admit. We explain the structural incentives that make consensus analysis systematically biased.
content:
Sell-side price targets are anchored to the current price far more than analysts admit.

Academic research on analyst forecasting has documented this for decades, yet the market continues to treat consensus targets as meaningful signals. Understanding why they are systematically biased is essential for any investor trying to generate independent alpha.

**The anchoring problem**

Studies consistently show that the average sell-side price target is set approximately 20-25% above the current share price — regardless of valuation fundamentals. This is not coincidence. It reflects the structural incentives of the sell-side model, where maintaining access to management and generating trading commissions takes precedence over forecast accuracy.

**The coverage bias**

Analysts rarely initiate coverage on companies they expect to underperform. Negative initiations damage relationships and generate no commission revenue. The result is a coverage universe that is structurally overweight buy recommendations.

**What to do instead**

Independent research starts from first principles: what is this business worth, and why does the current price differ from that value? The answer to the second question is usually more interesting than the first.

title: Rates, Duration & the Equity Risk Premium
excerpt: With long-end yields stabilising, the valuation framework for equities is shifting again. We revisit the equity risk premium and what it implies for sector allocation.
content:
With long-end yields stabilising, the valuation framework for equities is shifting again.

The relationship between rates and equity valuations is more nuanced than the simple inverse correlation that dominated market commentary in 2022. Duration sensitivity varies enormously across sectors, and the equity risk premium — properly measured — tells a different story than headline P/E multiples suggest.

**The ERP today**

Using a trailing earnings yield minus the 10-year real yield, the ERP currently sits at approximately 2.8% — below its long-run average of 3.5% but well above the sub-2% readings that preceded the 2000 and 2007 corrections.

This is not a screaming buy signal, but it is not a warning either. It suggests equities are fairly valued relative to bonds at current yield levels, with the balance of risk depending on earnings trajectory.

**Sector implications**

High-duration growth stocks remain vulnerable to any further yield backup. Real asset-backed businesses — infrastructure, energy, select industrials — offer better protection against the inflation scenarios that would push yields higher. We continue to favour quality compounders with pricing power over terminal value stories.

title: Initiating Coverage: UK Small-Cap Compounders
excerpt: Three UK-listed companies with returns on capital above 20%, low analyst coverage, and share prices that have gone nowhere for two years. One looks particularly interesting.
content:
Three UK-listed companies with returns on capital above 20%, low analyst coverage, and share prices that have gone nowhere for two years.

The UK small-cap market remains one of the most inefficiently priced corners of the developed world. A combination of domestic investor underallocation, post-Brexit institutional neglect, and index exclusion has created a pool of high-quality businesses trading at material discounts to their intrinsic value.

**Our screening criteria**

We screened for companies with: ROCE above 20% in each of the last 5 years; market cap between £50m and £500m; fewer than 5 active sell-side analysts; and share price within 10% of its 2-year low.

The screen returned 11 names. We have conducted detailed analysis on three of them.

**The standout**

One name in particular combines an exceptional returns profile with a management team that has consistently bought back stock at low valuations and avoided dilutive acquisitions. At current prices it trades at 11x normalised earnings — a 40% discount to the sector median. We are initiating with a buy recommendation and a 12-month price target implying 45% upside.

title: Energy Transition Capex: Who Pays?
excerpt: The investment required for net-zero is well-documented. Less discussed is which parts of the value chain will fund it — and who will end up holding the stranded assets.
content:
The investment required for net-zero is well-documented. Less discussed is which parts of the value chain will fund it — and who will end up holding the stranded assets.

BloombergNEF estimates $200 trillion of cumulative energy investment is required by 2050. The political consensus on the destination is reasonably clear. The financing mechanism is not.

**The stranded asset risk**

Utilities are being asked to accelerate grid investment at the same time that their existing asset base faces accelerated obsolescence. The regulated return framework in most European markets does not adequately compensate for this dual risk — which is why we remain cautious on regulated utilities despite their apparently attractive dividend yields.

**Where the opportunity lies**

The picks-and-shovels approach to energy transition — grid components, transformer manufacturers, cable producers — offers exposure to the capex cycle without the stranded asset risk. These businesses have order books extending 3-5 years and pricing power they have not enjoyed in a generation.

We continue to find better risk-reward in the equipment and infrastructure layer than in the generation assets themselves.

title: First Post: Why We Started Hawthorne & Fletcher
excerpt: Independent research exists because conflicts of interest are structural, not accidental. This is why we started this firm.
content:
Independent research exists because conflicts of interest are structural, not accidental.

**The problem with sell-side research**

Most equity research is produced by banks that also underwrite the companies being covered. The incentive to maintain relationships with issuers creates a systematic bias toward positive recommendations that is well-documented in academic literature.

**Why independence matters**

At Hawthorne & Fletcher, our only client is the investor. We have no banking relationships, no corporate access arrangements, and no incentive to tell you anything other than what our analysis concludes.

**What to expect**

We will publish research on a regular basis covering individual equities, sectors, and macro themes. Every piece will show our reasoning in full — so you can agree or disagree with our conclusions on the merits.
